# Rooftop solar installation: project proposal

## Case

This proposal sets out the case for installing a rooftop solar installation on the building, and it is intended to provide the reader with a comprehensive overview of the background to the project, the reasoning that supports it, and the various considerations that have ultimately led to the recommendation that is being put forward here. The building has a roof that is currently not being used for the generation of electricity, and it is felt that this represents something of a missed opportunity, in the sense that the same roof area could potentially be used to generate electricity on the site where that electricity is used. Rooftop generation of this kind has the advantage that the electricity is produced at the point of use, and the installation makes use of an existing surface rather than requiring additional land to be taken up for the purpose. The case, therefore, is essentially that the site already possesses a suitable surface, that the technology for generating electricity on such a surface is well established and widely deployed, and that a project of this nature would allow the organisation to generate a portion of its electricity on its own premises rather than relying entirely on supplies brought in from outside. It should also be noted that the case being made at this stage is a case for proceeding with the next stage of work on the project, and it is not being suggested that every detail of the installation has already been settled or that the organisation is in a position to commit itself to the construction of the installation on the basis of the information that is currently available. A considerable amount of further work would still need to be undertaken before any such commitment could responsibly be made, and the purpose of the material that follows is to explain what that further work is and why it is considered to be worth doing.

## Costs

In terms of the costs of the project, the headline figure that has been arrived at at this preliminary stage is a capital cost of $1031k, and this figure should be regarded as the central figure around which the financial appraisal of the project has been structured. The appraisal of the project has been carried out over a 7-year appraisal horizon, and this horizon provides the frame within which the costs of the proposal have been considered for the purposes of this document. It is worth emphasising that the capital cost quoted here is the figure that is available at this early stage of the project's development, and figures of this kind are inevitably subject to refinement as the design of the installation is developed in greater detail and as the various elements that will make up the installation are specified more precisely. For that reason, the costs section of this proposal should be read as presenting the order of the financial commitment that the detailed design stage would be working with, rather than as presenting a final and fixed price for the completed installation. The purpose of setting out the capital cost and the appraisal horizon together is to give the reader a clear sense of the scale of the proposal, and to make it possible to judge whether a commitment of this scale is one that the organisation wishes to explore further through the detailed design work that is being requested. It is also intended that the detailed design stage, if it is approved, will return to the question of costs and will present them in a more developed form, at which point a further decision can be taken in the light of that more detailed information.

## Schedule

Turning to the question of the schedule for the project, the intention is that work would be able to start one quarter after approval is given, and this timing should be understood as the planned starting point for the next stage of the work rather than as a guaranteed date that has been fixed with any external party. At this stage of the proceedings, no contractor is named in this proposal, and no commitment has been entered into with any contractor in relation to this project, so the schedule that is presented here is necessarily expressed in terms of the organisation's own approval process rather than in terms of dates that have been agreed elsewhere. The interval of one quarter between approval and the start of work is intended to allow the necessary internal arrangements to be put in place in an orderly way, so that the detailed design work, when it begins, can proceed on a properly prepared footing. It should be appreciated that the schedule beyond that starting point has not been developed in detail in this document, precisely because the detailed sequencing of the work is itself one of the products that the detailed design stage would be expected to produce. The reader is therefore asked to note the proposed starting interval, and to treat the remainder of the programme as a matter that will be reported back once the detailed design has been undertaken and the associated planning has been carried out.

## Decision requested

In conclusion, the decision that is being requested by this proposal is approval to proceed to detailed design, and it is important to be clear that what is being asked for is not approval to proceed to construction. These are two quite separate decisions, and the distinction between them is a significant one, because the detailed design stage is the stage at which the open questions that have been identified in this document can be worked through and at which the costs and the schedule can be placed on a firmer footing. By approving the move to detailed design, the reader would be authorising the next stage of investigation and development work, and would not be committing the organisation to building the installation, which would remain a matter for a separate and subsequent decision taken in the light of the detailed design and its findings. It is hoped that the material set out above provides a sufficient basis for that decision to be taken, and the recommendation is therefore that approval to proceed to detailed design be granted, with the question of construction reserved for a later stage once the detailed design work has been completed and reported.

# Rooftop solar installation: project proposal

## Case

Approval is requested to proceed to detailed design for a rooftop solar installation. Construction is not requested. The building has a roof that is not used to generate electricity. Generation on that roof would produce electricity at the point of use and would use an existing surface; no additional land is required. The case for the next stage rests on those two properties of the site and on the state of the design: the surface is available, the technology is established, and the open questions are questions of design detail rather than of principle. The case is not a case for construction. The installation is not yet specified in detail, the costs stand at a preliminary figure, and the schedule is expressed relative to approval. Each of those items is a product of the detailed design stage. The proposal therefore asks for the stage that settles them, and it holds the construction decision separate, to be taken on the detailed design and its costs when they are reported. Nothing in the case depends on a benefit that the detailed design has not yet established. The roof area, the point of use, and the absence of a land requirement are properties of the site as it stands. The generation that the installation would deliver, the layout that the roof can carry, and the connection arrangements are not properties of the site as it stands, and this proposal does not state them. A reader who accepts the case accepts a narrower proposition than a reader who approves a construction project: that a site with an unused roof at the point of use justifies the cost of a detailed design. The alternative to the detailed design is a decision taken on preliminary figures, and the preliminary figures in the costs section show why that alternative is weak. The capital figure is a single estimate at an early stage. The appraisal horizon is stated so that the scale of the commitment can be judged, not so that a return can be asserted. Where a proposal of this kind is refused at the design stage, the refusal is normally on scale or on priority, and both grounds are visible in this document: the scale is stated in the costs section, and the priority judgement is the reader's. The case section adds one further ground for proceeding. Electricity generated on the roof is generated behind the site's own point of use, so the installation's output displaces supply that the site would otherwise take in. That property does not depend on the detailed design either. It follows from the location of the generation, and it holds for any layout the detailed design may settle on. The case, stated in full, is that the site offers a suitable surface at the point of use, that the remaining questions are design questions, and that the design stage is the proportionate next step for a commitment of the stated scale. A further consideration supports the same step. A detailed design is reversible in a way construction is not. If the design returns figures the organisation does not accept, the project stops at the design report, and the loss is the design work alone. The structure of the request is therefore staged: a bounded commitment now, the information that a construction decision requires, and the construction decision itself reserved until that information exists. Proposals that merge the two decisions force the reader to judge construction on design-stage evidence, and the separation maintained here is the reason the request can be decided on the material in this document.

## Costs

Capital cost is $1031k. The appraisal horizon is 7 years. The capital figure is the figure available at this stage and it is preliminary: the design is not yet developed, the elements of the installation are not yet specified, and a figure set before specification is refined as specification proceeds. The figure is stated so that the scale of the commitment can be judged before the detailed design is approved. It is the number the detailed design will work from and the number it will replace with a developed cost. The horizon performs the same function for time. The appraisal period bounds the comparison the reader is asked to make: costs and benefits beyond the horizon are outside the appraisal as presented, and a reader who appraises over a longer period is making a different comparison from the one this document sets out. No return figure is stated in this proposal. A return would require a generation figure, and generation depends on the layout, the orientation in detail, and the equipment the detailed design selects. Stating a return on the preliminary capital figure would present a precision the project does not yet have. The costs section therefore states what is known (the preliminary capital cost), the frame in which it is appraised (the horizon), and what is not yet stated (any return, any operating figure, any breakdown of the capital sum). The breakdown belongs to the detailed design, which will present the cost by element, on a specified design, and will return the question of construction to the reader with that breakdown in hand. The decision requested at this stage is priced by the capital figure only in scale. Approval of detailed design commits the organisation to the design work, not to construction at the stated capital scale, and the distinction is stated again in the decision section because the two commitments are easily confused. The capital cost is the scale of the project that the design would define. It is not the cost of the approval being requested.

## Schedule

Work starts one quarter after approval. No contractor is named. The schedule is stated relative to the approval because no commitment exists outside the organisation's own process: there is no agreed date with any external party, and a calendar date would imply one. The quarter between approval and the start of work is the interval for internal arrangements, so that the detailed design begins on a prepared footing. No programme beyond that start is stated. The sequencing of the design work, its stages, and its reporting points are products of the work itself, and a programme set out now would be a programme for a design that has not been specified. The detailed design will report its own schedule for the stages that follow it, including the schedule on which a construction decision could be taken and the schedule construction would follow if approved. The reader is asked to fix one interval only: approval, then one quarter, then the start of design work. That interval also protects the decision itself. A start tied to approval rather than to a date means a deferred decision defers the start by the same amount, and the project does not drift into work that the decision has not yet authorised.

## Decision requested

The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design. Approval to proceed to construction is not requested and is not given by this decision. The detailed design will settle the layout the roof can carry, the equipment, the connection arrangements, a developed cost by element, and a programme for the stages after design. On that report, construction becomes a separate decision, taken on specified figures. Approval at this stage authorises design work. It commits the organisation to that work and to nothing beyond it.
